question: How many cups of tea do people in the United Kingdom drink per day?

target.what: Total number of cups of tea consumed by people in the United Kingdom (England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland) in a single day, counting each cup/teacup/mug serving of tea (hot brewed tea, including herbal/fruit and green tea, but excluding iced tea and ready-to-drink bottled tea unless explicitl
target.publisher: No single official publisher; candidate sources include the UK Tea & Infusions Association (UKTIA), Defra Family Food survey, ONS, Kantar/Nielsen retail data, and trade bodies
target.cadence: Irregular / ad hoc; no official daily series exists
target.caveats: Ambiguous: 'cups' could mean standard teacups (~190-250 ml) or mugs (~250-350 ml); could include or exclude herbal/fruit teas, iced tea, out-of-home consumption, and non-residents. Working interpretation: all hot tea servings by all people physically in the UK on the reference day, using a standard

candidates.hypothesis: UKTIA and press frequently cite a headline 'X million cups of tea a day' figure for the UK. If such a published estimate exists, it directly anchors the target (possibly the single best evidence). Direction: target ≈ published daily cups figure, adjusted for definitional scope (herbal inclusion, out-of-home).
candidates.data_to_find: Any UKTIA, trade press, or news-reported figure for 'cups of tea drunk per day in the UK' with its date and stated definition; also the underlying per-capita cups/day and population used. Substitute: per-capita cups/day from survey sources.

candidates.hypothesis: Total cups/day = UK population × average cups per person per day. Per-capita tea consumption can be derived from Defra Family Food / ONS household consumption data (tea purchases or intake) converted to cups via average cup size. Direction: target scales linearly with population and per-capita rate.
candidates.data_to_find: UK population estimate for 2026 (ONS); per-capita tea consumption (kg/person/year or cups/person/day) from Defra Family Food, NDNS, or Kantar; average grams of tea per cup to convert. Minimum: one per-capita rate and one population figure.

candidates.hypothesis: Cups/day ≈ (UK tea supply available for domestic consumption per day) ÷ (grams of tea per cup). Supply = imports + domestic production − exports ± stock change, from HMRC trade data and FAO/ITC. Direction: target proportional to net tea availability and inversely proportional to tea-per-cup.
candidates.data_to_find: UK tea imports and exports (tonnes/year) from HMRC/UN Comtrade; domestic production negligible; stock changes; grams of dry tea per cup (typically ~2-3 g, lower for tea bags/reuse). Minimum: annual net availability in tonnes and a g/cup factor.

assessment.note: Two independent headline estimates of UK daily tea cups: UKTIA 'over 100 million' (p49) and Aldi/Perspectus '127 million' (p86). Both are trade/press figures with unclear methodology, but they bracket a plausible range and are the most direct anchors. They are not independent of each other in the sense that both likely derive from similar industry assumptions, but they come from different publishers.

YouGov (p62, p64) and UKTIA/Crave (p75) both indicate high tea participation: 74% drink weekly, 25% never, and >90% drink at least one cup a day (p75). The p75 figure is likely overstated due to survey framing, but directionally consistent with high penetration.

Defra Family Food data: 19 g/person/week tea purchased at home in 2023 (p13, p127) and total beverages 49 g/person/week (p138). These are consistent with declining tea purchases and provide a physical-flow basis for at-home consumption.
Out-of-home tea consumption series from Defra: 12 ml/person/week in 2023 (p14), 30 ml in 2014 (p20), 44 ml in 2004 (p21). Shows a declining trend but provides a small out-of-home volume component.

Beverage Standards Association: average tea drinker has 2 cups out-of-home on a weekday (p34) and 1 on a weekend (p35). These are per-drinker, not per-capita, and from 2017, but useful for out-of-home share.

Surveys on cups per drinker per day conflict: p22/p33 say 35% drink 3+ cups/day; p76 says 35% drink 3-4 cups; p77 says 44% drink 1-2 cups; p78 says 20% drink 5-6 cups. These are from different surveys with different question wording and may not be directly comparable, but they suggest a wide range of per-drinker consumption.

Aldi/Perspectus survey: average 4 cups/day per person (p85), 72% drink average 4 cups/day (p88), 1,460 cups/year per Brit (p89). These are internally consistent but likely overstate per-capita consumption because they may refer to tea drinkers or use a leading question.
ONS population estimates: 69.5 million mid-2025 (p111) and 69,483,900 for 2025 (p119). These are consistent and provide the population denominator.

UK tea imports: 53,000 tonnes in H1 2023 (p23) and Kenya alone 30,100 tonnes (p28). These are consistent with import volumes and can be used for a physical-flow estimate, though they include re-exports and not all imports are consumed as tea.

a3.role: out-of-home tea cups per person per day

methods.rationale: Physical-flow route: at-home tea purchases (p13) converted to cups using grams per cup (a1) and a consumption share (a2), plus out-of-home cups (a3). This gives per-capita cups/day; multiplying by population (p111 or p119) would give total, but the formula as written gives per-capita. To get total, we would need to multiply by population. However, the target is total cups/day, so we should include population. The formula currently gives per-capita; we need to multiply by population. Let's adjust: formula should be (p13 * k_days_per_week / a1) * a2 * p111 + a3 * p111. But that would be total. Alternatively, we can use p111 as population. Let's revise: formula = ((p13 * k_days_per_week / a1) * a2 + a3) * p111. But p111 is total population, and p13 is per person per week, so multiplying by population gives total weekly cups, then divide by 7 to get daily? Actually p13 is per week, so (p13 * k_days_per_week / a1) gives cups per person per week? No: p13 is grams per person per week. Dividing by a1 (g/cup) gives cups per person per week. Multiplying by a2 gives consumed cups per person per week. Then adding a3 (cups per person per day) is inconsistent units. We need to convert a3 to per week: a3 * k_days_per_week. So formula: (p13 / a1) * a2 + a3 * k_days_per_week gives cups per person per week. Then multiply by population and divide by k_days_per_week to get cups per day. That simplifies to ((p13 / a1) * a2 / k_days_per_week + a3) * population. But k_days_per_week is 7, so (p13/a1)*a2/7 gives cups per person per day from at-home. Then plus a3 gives total per person per day. Then multiply by population. So formula: ((p13 / a1) * a2 / k_days_per_week + a3) * p111. This uses p111 (population). Let's use p111 (69.5 million). The formula is: ((p13 / a1) * a2 / k_days_per_week + a3) * p111. This yields total cups/day. Unit: cups/day. We'll use p111 as population. Note: p13 is 2023 data, p111 is 2025 population; we assume per-capita tea purchase rate is stable from 2023 to 2026. This is a limitation. Also, p13 is household purchases, which may exclude some out-of-home; we add a3 for out-of-home. The formula uses a1, a2, a3 assumptions. This method is a full estimate.

methods.rationale: Base-rate decomposition: population (p111) times share who drink tea (a4) times average cups per drinker per day (a5). This is a standard Fermi approach. It relies on survey-based participation and per-drinker consumption, which are uncertain but independent of the physical-flow route. The main weakness is that a4 and a5 are assumptions derived from conflicting surveys; the wide ranges reflect that uncertainty.

p86.role: Aldi calculated UK cups of tea per day

methods.rationale: Direct headline estimates: average of UKTIA's 'over 100 million' (p49) and Aldi's '127 million' (p86). These are the most direct published figures for the target, though both are trade/press estimates with unclear methodology. Averaging them gives a central anchor. The uncertainty is set by code's lognormal assumption for data points, but the true uncertainty is likely larger due to definitional issues (e.g., cup size, inclusion of herbal tea).

assumptions.name: Grams of tea per cup (dry leaf equivalent)
assumptions.rationale: UKTIA uses 3g per cup for global conversion (p60), but UK tea bags typically contain 2-3g and mugs may use one bag. A range of 1.8-3.5g covers weak to strong brews and different bag sizes.
assumptions.applies_when: Converting dry tea mass to cups for at-home consumption; assumes all tea mass is brewed and consumed as hot tea.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that UK tea bags are consistently larger (e.g., 3.5g+) or that significant tea is wasted or used for iced tea.

assumptions.name: Share of at-home tea purchases consumed as hot tea (not wasted or iced)
assumptions.rationale: Most tea purchased for home is brewed as hot tea; some waste (unused bags, overbrewing) and iced tea use is minor. 90% is a reasonable central estimate.
assumptions.applies_when: Converting household tea purchases to cups; excludes out-of-home.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence of significant household tea waste or iced tea production from retail tea.

assumptions.name: Out-of-home tea cups per person per day (UK average)
assumptions.rationale: Defra out-of-home tea consumption was 12 ml/person/week in 2023 (p14), which at ~200 ml/cup is ~0.06 cups/day, but this likely undercounts workplace and café tea. Beverage Standards Association data (p34-p35) suggest tea drinkers have 1-2 cups out-of-home on weekdays, but only a fraction of people drink out-of-home daily. 0.3 cups/person/day is a compromise.
assumptions.applies_when: Adding out-of-home component to at-home estimate; assumes out-of-home tea is additional to at-home.
assumptions.falsified_by: Survey evidence showing average out-of-home tea consumption is much lower (e.g., <0.1 cups/day) or much higher (>0.6).

assumptions.name: Share of UK population that drinks tea (any frequency)
assumptions.rationale: YouGov (p62, p64) found 74% drink tea at least weekly and 25% never; UKTIA (p75) claims >90% drink at least one cup a day, which is likely overstated. 75% is consistent with YouGov.
assumptions.applies_when: Used in base-rate decomposition; assumes non-drinkers consume zero cups.
assumptions.falsified_by: A representative survey showing tea participation below 65% or above 85%.

assumptions.name: Average cups per tea drinker per day
assumptions.rationale: Surveys conflict: p22/p33 say 35% drink 3+ cups/day; p76 says 35% drink 3-4 cups; p77 says 44% drink 1-2 cups; p78 says 20% drink 5-6 cups. methods.label: m2

p176.role: average cups of tea per Briton per week (YouGov 2015)

methods.rationale: Population times survey-based weekly cups converted to daily. Uses the 2015 YouGov 17 cups/week mean; per-capita tea consumption has declined since, so this likely overstates 2026, but it is a transparent survey-based route.

methods.label: m4

a4.role: at-home cups per person per day

a3.role: out-of-home cups per person per day

methods.rationale: Bottom-up per-capita decomposition summing at-home (derived from Defra household purchase data p13/p127) and out-of-home (from p34/p35/p162) channels, times population. This is the most defensible structural route and avoids the over-reporting of survey means.

methods.label: m5

p49.role: UKTIA stated UK cups of tea per day

methods.rationale: Direct anchor to the UKTIA trade-body headline of over 100 million cups/day. It is a rounded, undated claim of unknown derivation, but it is the single most-cited published estimate and serves as a central reference.

excluded_by_input_audit.label: m3
excluded_by_input_audit.reason: input audit: p208: Black tea imports are a supply/import quantity, not domestic consumption; imports include re-exports and exclude domestic production/stock changes, so it is a different quantity than UK tea cons

kept.name: Share of UK black-tea imports actually brewed into domestic cups (net of re-export, waste, non-beverage use)
kept.rationale: Imports include re-exports and some industrial/non-beverage use; most imported black tea is brewed in UK homes and cafés. Wide range reflects stock changes and re-export uncertainty.
kept.applies_when: Used to convert black-tea import mass into cups drunk in the UK.
kept.falsified_by: Evidence of a large re-export share or substantial non-beverage tea use in the UK.

kept.name: Average grams of tea per cup (UK domestic brewing)
kept.rationale: UKTIA uses 3 g/cup globally; UK tea bags are typically ~2-2.5 g and mugs are larger, so a slightly lower per-cup mass is plausible. Range spans tea-bag to loose-leaf/mug practice.
kept.applies_when: Converting tea mass to cup servings for UK domestic consumption.
kept.falsified_by: Documented UK average tea-bag mass or brewing strength materially outside this range.

kept.name: Out-of-home tea cups per person per day (all UK population)
kept.rationale: p34/p35 give 1-2 cups/day among out-of-home tea drinkers, but only ~16% of tea drinkers buy out-of-home weekly (p162); averaging over the whole population yields a small per-capita out-of-home rate.
kept.applies_when: Added to at-home per-capita rate to cover the out-of-home channel.
kept.falsified_by: Survey showing a much larger share of the population regularly drinking tea out of home.

kept.name: Average at-home cups per person per day implied by household purchase data
kept.rationale: p13/p127 give 19 g/person/week; at ~2.5 g/cup this is ~7.6 cups/week ≈ 1.1 cups/day, but household purchase data under-record some consumption; range reflects cup-mass and under-recording uncertainty.
kept.applies_when: Used as the at-home component of a bottom-up per-capita estimate.
kept.falsified_by: Evidence that household purchase data substantially under- or over-state actual brewed cups.

residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.
